issues.legal_issue: A trustee is not liable for compound interest on trust funds merely because the funds may have been used in the trustee’s business when such use has not been proved.
material_facts: The case concerned the accounting of funds held by a trustee of a public temple.
The lower court found no dishonest misappropriation, and the record contained no clear finding or evidence that the funds had been used in the trustee’s business.
The pleadings did not allege that the funds had been used in the trustee’s business.
issues.conclusion: The trustee was not liable to pay compound interest because it had not been proved that the trust funds were used in the trustee’s business.
issues.legal_principle: Compound interest could not be imposed on the equitable ground that the trustee used or mixed the trust funds with personal business funds where that factual basis was not proved. The court therefore rejected the High Court’s inference as insufficient to support compound interest.

predicates.public_trust_accounting_case: The proceeding seeks an accounting of funds held by a trustee for a public trust.
predicates.trust_funds_used_in_business_proved: Evidence establishes that the trustee used the trust funds in the trustee’s business.

issues.definition: When a public-trust accounting proceeding does not establish that the trustee used the trust funds in business, the trustee is not liable for compound interest on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A trustee who retains trust funds uninvested for an unreasonable time, when they are not required for current trust purposes, is liable to pay simple interest on them.
material_facts: The trustee retained a substantial balance of trust funds uninvested for more than twenty years.
The accounts showed that the funds could not reasonably have been expected to be required for the trust’s current purposes during that period.
No applicable statute governing public charitable trusts provided for the trustee’s liability to pay interest.
issues.conclusion: The trustee was liable to pay simple interest at four per cent per annum on the trust funds retained uninvested.
issues.legal_principle: In the absence of an applicable statutory rule, interest could be imposed on equitable grounds where a trustee ought to have received interest, including where the trustee leaves trust money uninvested for an unreasonable time. A trustee must act as an ordinarily prudent person of business would with their own affairs. Halsbury’s Laws of England, third edition, volume 38, paragraphs 1691, 1812 and 1814, supported liability for interest and the general application of simple interest at four per cent where trust money is simply left uninvested. The Indian Trusts Act did not apply to public or private religious or charitable endowments, and the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act contained no provision imposing interest liability.

predicates.public_trust_accounting_case: The proceeding seeks an accounting of funds held by a trustee for a public trust.
predicates.trustee_retained_trust_funds_uninvested_: The trustee kept trust funds uninvested for an unreasonable length of time.
predicates.funds_not_needed_for_current_trust_purpo: The funds were not reasonably expected to be needed for the trust’s current purposes during that time.

issues.definition: When a trustee in a public-trust accounting proceeding unreasonably keeps funds uninvested that are not needed for current trust purposes, the trustee is liable for simple interest.

issues.legal_issue: The rule of damdupat does not limit interest imposed on a trustee’s equitable liability for trust funds because the trustee did not borrow those funds from the trust.
material_facts: The funds were in the trustee’s custody as trust funds, rather than having been advanced to the trustee as a loan.
The trustee’s liability to pay interest arose from the court’s equitable assessment of the trustee’s failure to invest the funds.
The interest calculated at the applicable simple rate exceeded the principal, and the trustee sought to limit it under the rule of damdupat.
issues.conclusion: The rule of damdupat did not apply to the interest payable by the trustee, even though that interest exceeded the principal.
issues.legal_principle: The rule of damdupat concerns interest on a loan advanced by a creditor to a borrower and does not extend to interest awarded equitably against a trustee who, as an individual, did not borrow funds from himself as trustee. Colebrooke’s Digest on Hindu Law describes the rule in the context of loans and creditor-debtor relations. The court referred to Sharp v. Jackson and Lake, In re Dyer, Ex Parte, in considering whether a trustee may be described as a debtor; it held that even if a trustee’s liability to restore misused funds may be described as a debt, the trustee is not thereby a borrower. The court also referred to Dhondu Jagannath v. Narayan Ramchandra in describing the rule’s operation in loan cases.

predicates.public_trust_accounting_case: The proceeding concerns a trustee’s accounting for funds held for a public trust.
predicates.trustee_had_custody_of_funds_without_rec: The trustee held the funds in a fiduciary capacity and did not receive them as a loan from the trust.
predicates.interest_liability_arose_equity: The court imposed interest because of the trustee’s equitable responsibility for the funds, rather than because of a loan agreement.

issues.definition: When a trustee held trust funds without borrowing them and the interest liability arose in equity, the rule of damdupat does not limit that interest.
